Seema, you know what's strange? I used to be the loudest person in our team meetings. Now I just nod. Since Kunal became our lead, he eats lunch with the other managers, answers my messages with one word, and last month he said, "Let's keep ideas to the agenda, Madhuri," in front of everyone. I felt like a schoolgirl.
So I stopped. Two weeks ago I noticed the vendor's figures didn't match ours. Old me would have raised it in the meeting. New me thought, why bother, he'll just think I'm showing off. I told nobody.
It blew up on Friday. The client caught it. Kunal was furious and asked why nobody had flagged it. I sat there with my face hot. I had flagged it, in my head.
The whole team has gone quiet like that. It's not a stronger team, Seema. It's just a quieter one.

Would it sound like sulking? He said nothing. Two others stared at their laptops too. The meeting ended in eleven minutes, the quietest they had ever had.

Jaya, you say your old batchmate is now your manager and you've stopped talking in meetings. Let me tell you about the year my friend Kamala became head clerk at the post office where we both worked. We had shared tiffin every day for five years.
The week she was promoted, she began eating at the superintendent's table. When I pointed out a mistake in the money-order register, she said, "I'll decide what's a mistake now, Pallavi." I went home and cried into my pillow, silly girl that I was.
After that, I kept my mouth shut. So did the others. When the register didn't tally in March, all six of us had seen it coming. Not one of us said a word. Kamala faced the inquiry alone, and we sat at our desks feeling guilty and, I'm ashamed to say, a little glad.
That silence cost all of us something. Think about that before you swallow your next idea.

qa.a: Pallavi and the others chose silence after feeling dropped, so no one flagged the register before it failed to tally.

qa.a: Kamala probably felt shocked and isolated, realising the colleagues who once warned her had stopped speaking up.

At 1 a.m., two hours before the app update was due to go live, the office generator coughed and the lights dimmed. Varun, lead for four months, was pacing between desks when Samir said, "The login change hasn't been tested on slow networks. I think we should hold the release a day."
Varun didn't stop pacing. "You always find a reason to slow things down, Samir."
"I'm saying it because half our users are in small towns."
"And I'm saying it because I can see the bigger picture." Varun looked round the room. "Some people just aren't comfortable with speed."
Samir turned back to his screen. Nobody else spoke.
In the cab home at 4 a.m., after pressing release, Varun replayed the moment. Samir had always been a bit jealous, hadn't he? Ever since the promotion. That was all it was. He felt a knot in his stomach and decided it was tiredness.

qa.q: What had not been tested, according to Samir?
qa.a: The login change, on slow networks.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he decided Samir was jealous?
qa.a: He felt threatened and uneasy, with a knot in his stomach, and protected his new image by calling the warning jealousy.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Varun at this stage?
qa.a: He could call Samir the next day, ask exactly what worried him, and test the login on slow networks before users complain.

qa.q: How might Samir feel after being told he always slows things down?
qa.a: Samir probably feels dismissed and embarrassed in front of the team, and less willing to raise concerns next time.

grounding: Under release-night pressure, a new lead brushes off a warning as jealousy and a lack of nerve, protecting his image and learning nothing.

In the weekly review at their Kolkata office, Rekha said carefully, "Jagdish, the client's research says their buyers are over fifty. The campaign we're pitching is all short videos for teenagers. I'm worried we're missing them."
Jagdish smiled the smile he had started using since becoming lead. "That's exactly the old thinking this client wants to escape, Rekha. Vision means seeing where they should go, not where they are."
Two juniors nodded. Rekha said nothing more.
Later, a senior designer raised the same concern at the coffee machine. Jagdish laughed. "Everyone suddenly has opinions now that I'm lead." He went back to his desk and wrote in his notebook: Team resisting change. Needs stronger direction.
He didn't open the research file again. He had read it once, before the promotion.

Today was bad. The event is delayed by a week because the sound vendor I picked backed out. I chose them alone, fast, because they were cheapest and I wanted to show I could decide. I didn't ask Samir, who has handled vendors for three years.
On the client call I said, "The team didn't check their availability properly." The team. Me. I saw Samir's face on the screen when I said it. He just looked down.
Afterwards the director asked me directly who had approved the vendor. I said, "I did." My voice came out small.
I keep replaying it. Two months ago people called me the golden one. Today I felt like a fraud in a borrowed chair. My hands are still shaky as I write this.
I owe Samir something. I don't know what yet.

When Suraj became supervisor of the village milk-collection centre, he moved the morning pickup from six to eight without asking anyone. It would save one tanker trip, he told the cooperative, and they praised him for it.
Raghav, who had run the chilling unit for twelve years, had said once, quietly, "In May, two hours matters." Suraj had waved it off.
On the third hot morning the tanker was late, and eight hundred litres turned sour in the cans. Farmers crowded the gate, shouting. The cooperative chairman arrived on his scooter.
"The staff didn't switch on the chiller in time," Suraj said at once.
Raghav stood holding the logbook, the chiller times written in his neat hand. He didn't argue. He just held it out.
Suraj looked at the numbers, then at the farmers. The back of his neck went cold. For the first time since the promotion, he didn't know what to say.

Usha, the hardest meeting of my life? A Monday in March, eight months into being team lead. I'd pushed a new delivery rota through without asking anyone, and it tangled our routes for two weeks. At first, I'm ashamed to say, I told the regional head the drivers weren't adapting.
That Monday I stood in front of all thirty of them in the depot. My mouth was dry. I said, "The rota was my decision. I didn't ask you. Pinto warned me and I didn't listen. I'm sorry for blaming you." Then I asked, "What should I have asked before?"
Silence. Then Pinto, the oldest driver, said, "Ask us about school timings, sir." And they started talking. Forty minutes.
Here's the strange part. After that day they trusted me more, not less. I'm Chinmay, and I learned more in that depot than in any training.

I've worked under three leads, and I've never seen what Hafsa did at Thursday's all-hands.
The product had shipped with a bug that locked out two hundred customers for a day. Everyone knew Zainab had flagged the risk a week earlier, and that Hafsa had pushed the release anyway. On Tuesday Hafsa had muttered something about testing being slow, so I expected more of that.
Instead she put up a single slide: My call. My mistake. She said Zainab had warned her, clearly and on time, and thanked her by name. Then she said, "Tell me when I'm doing this again. My calendar's open. Book twenty minutes and be blunt."
I couldn't tell how she felt. Her voice was steady, but she held the clicker tight.
By Friday her calendar was full. People talked about her differently at lunch. Better, I think.

You once told me a lead's real job is to be a good plumber: find what's blocked and clear it. I didn't get it when you said it. I think I do now.
When I took over the team in January, I spent the first month in meetings making decisions. The team got quieter. So I changed. Every Monday I now ask everyone one question: what's in your way this week? Last week it was a broken test server, a vendor who wasn't replying, and Ramesh's leave that kept getting stuck in approval. I spent my week on those three things. Nothing glamorous.
When the director praised our release, I named the four people who built it. I still eat lunch with the old gang on Thursdays; they tease me more than ever.
Ramesh runs the stand-ups now, and he's better at it than I was.
Thank you for the plumbing lesson.
Shankar

Gurleen, you've just been made lead, so let me tell you what I'd do differently if I started again. For my first three months I thought leading meant being the smartest person in the room. My team went quiet. Nobody told me when things went wrong.
What changed it was small. I started ending every one-to-one with, "What can I get out of your way?" Once it was a laptop that kept crashing. Once it was a client who kept calling my junior at midnight. I dealt with those things. That was the job.
I also stopped saying "I" in reports. It's "Neeraj built this, Shabnam tested that." And I still sit at our old table at lunch, where I sat as a junior, because those people tell me the truth.
A title gets people to listen for a week. What I do for them gets them to listen for years. I'm Pooja, and that's the one leadership lesson I really trust.

At the panchayat function, the new cluster coordinator, Anand, stood at the microphone and talked about the rainwater tanks in the three village schools. "I planned them, I got the funds, I supervised the work," he said, and the sarpanch clapped.
Pradeep, the old headmaster who had trained Anand as a young teacher, sat in the second row and watched the three teachers at the back. Lakshmi had dug with the children every Saturday. Babu had fought the contractor for proper pipes. Both were looking at their feet.
